title: MB7-06755
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellants are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Uruguay and a permanent resident of Argentina. His wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Argentina.
The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms XXXX XXXX XXXX as the designated representative of her minor children.

The appellants are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The RPD determined that they are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The appellants filed no new documents in support of their appeal, and they are not requesting a hearing before the RAD. The appellants are asking the RAD to set aside the RPD's determination and allow their claims for refugee protection.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is allowed.

Before he left Argentina in March 2016, the male appellant and his family were living in Moreno, a suburb of the capital city, Buenos Aires. He was a dental surgeon and owned his own practice in central Moreno. His wife worked with him as a receptionist.

The male appellant states in his Basis of Claim Form that he initially became established in a disadvantaged neighbourhood (XXXX XXXX XXXX) in order to offer his services to a less wealthy segment of the population, which included a large number of gypsies. His wife's written narrative indicates that they were also working elsewhere at the same time.

The male appellant stated that, as the years went on, the gypsy community demanded that he provide more and more services free of charge. The male appellant alleged that the gypsy chief (the cacique) and his son XXXX intimidated him and threatened to kill him when he told them he had no openings to treat them or when he had to refer gypsy patients to colleagues for more specialized care.

In 2009, after XXXX threatened to kill him, they told the female appellant's father (a retired police officer) about their problems. He explained that the authorities would not accept their complaint without a witness or evidence. The appellants left XXXX XXXX XXXX for central Moreno, where they believed they would have fewer problems. However, the situation did not improve; the gypsies continued to pressure the male appellant to provide his services free of charge, or in exchange for goods.

The male appellant alleged that his wife received a telephone call from someone falsely claiming that her husband was being held hostage and demanding a ransom. A sister-in-law was allegedly also a victim of such a virtual kidnapping scheme.

The male appellant further alleges that his wife was near the school one day, along with other mothers and their children, when a car drove up to them and one of the occupants tried to abduct one of the children.

In 2014, the appellants considered leaving Argentina and moving to Uruguay, but the male appellant's family told them it was not the best option. The appellants allegedly learned that gypsies travel freely between the two countries and that there have been child abductions in Uruguay, as well as drug problems.

The appellants wanted to leave Argentina. They submitted an application to go to Finland, but were refused. The male appellant closed his practice at the end of 2015. They obtained a visa allowing them to travel to the United States, then came to Canada to claim refugee protection. Impugned decision

The RPD rejected the claims for refugee protection on May 18, 2017. The RPD found that the appellants had credibly established that they had provided dental services to the gypsy community in Aurora, that this community had demanded more and more services, and that they had used intimidation to back up their demands. The RPD also found it credible that they had endured the situation for as long as they could. However, the RPD concluded that the male appellant could return to Uruguay. The male appellant had not established that the proximity of Uruguay and the presence of gypsies in that country would enable "Cacique and XXXX" to find him there.

The RPD further concluded that, alternatively, the principal claimant and his family have an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mendonza and that it would not be unreasonable for them to move there. GROUNDS OF APPEAL Appellants' position

The appellants argue on appeal that the RPD's decision contains an error of law. They submit that the RPD committed a breach of procedural fairness by failing to provide adequate reasons for its decision.
Furthermore, the RPD erred in its assessment of the corroborating documentary evidence and in its conclusion that they have a viable IFA.

The Federal Court of Appeal ruled in Huruglica1 on the scope of appeals before the RAD. In analyzing the legislative provisions and reiterating Parliament's intent in creating the RAD, Justice Gauthier remarked as follows: [98] The RAD was essentially viewed as the safety net that would catch all mistakes made by the RPD, be it on the law or the facts.

The Federal Court of Appeal further ruled that findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, must be reviewed applying the correctness standard. Where findings of fact or mixed fact and law require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence, the RPD may, in some cases, enjoy a meaningful advantage over the RAD. The Court of Appeal further ruled that the level of deference owed to the RPD in each case will vary and that the RAD should be given the opportunity to develop its own jurisprudence in that respect.

On May 23, 2017, the RAD rendered a split decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). In essence, my colleagues in the RAD were of the opinion that, "Where deference to findings of the RPD is warranted, the standard of RAD reasonableness will be applied." In their opinion, this standard must be adapted to the particular context of the RAD. They were further of the opinion that the RPD's findings must be "the result of a comprehensible reasoning process - the RAD must be able to read the RPD's decision and understand how the RPD's conclusion was reached." Finally, they stated that, "The RAD will consider the refugee determination on a standard of correctness, even where it has deferred to some or all of the findings upon which that determination is based."

Paragraph 171(c) of the IRPA states that a decision of a panel of three members of the RAD has, for the RPD and for a panel of one member of the RAD, the same precedential value as a decision of an appeal court has for a trial court.

Therefore, the RAD will conduct an independent analysis of the evidence in order to determine whether the RPD erred as the female appellant alleges. If the RPD erred in fact, in law, or in mixed fact and law, the RAD must intervene in accordance with sections 110 and 111 of the IRPA.

As counsel submits, these claims for refugee protection must be examined in relation to section 97 rather than section 96 of the IRPA. In order for section 96 to apply, the refugee protection claimant must have a well-founded fear based on one or more of the Convention grounds. The fact that the appellant provided professional services [translation] "free of charge" to gypsies has no nexus to any of the five Convention grounds.

The Supreme Court stated in Ward2 that the purpose of refugee protection is to defend human rights and to combat discrimination. The Court also set out three possible categories of particular social group: * groups defined by an innate, unchangeable characteristic; * groups whose members voluntarily associate for reasons so fundamental to their human dignity that they should not be forced to forsake the association; and * groups associated by a former voluntary status, unalterable due to its historical permanence.
The services the appellant provided to the gypsies, while laudable, do not correspond to the purpose the Supreme Court mentions in its decision.

The IFA in Mendonza, a city located 800 kilometres from Buenos Aires, is at the heart of this claim for refugee protection. An IFA is a question of mixed fact and law that must be reviewed on a correctness standard when it raises no issue of credibility.

Having carefully reviewed all the evidence and listened to the recording of the hearing, I am of the opinion that these claims must be re-determined by the RPD. The decision contains a fatal error in the second prong of the IFA analysis. I cannot correct this error without holding a hearing, and I must therefore refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination. My reasons follow.

I note from the decision that the factors considered in the IFA analysis are based on the fact that it would not be unreasonable for the male appellant and his family to relocate to that city. However, the male appellant is a citizen of Uruguay, and he must establish that he faces a prospective risk in his own country of citizenship. The IFA in Mendonza should be considered only if it has been established that his life is in danger in Uruguay.

In my opinion, the IFA in Mendonza can only be determinative for the female appellant and the children, who are citizens of Argentina. There is no evidence before me to show why Mendonza would not be a viable IFA for the female appellant and the children. I note from the recording of the hearing that she was not questioned about why she and the children could not move there, if she found work elsewhere than in her husband's practice. In my opinion, this error is fatal to the IFA analysis, specifically to the second prong of this analysis.

I am of the opinion that the determinative issue in these claims is state protection in Argentina for the female appellant and the children. I am also of the opinion that this is an important issue in the male appellant's claim. However, I cannot rule on this matter without questioning the appellants. The appellants' testimony regarding why they did not seek police protection in Argentina raises questions that I cannot resolve without a hearing.

For the foregoing reasons, I set aside the RPD's determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is allowed. Maria De Andrade Me Maria De Andrade October 24, 2017 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v.
